Robert Smalls. An enslaved maritime pilot who became a Civil War hero, Reconstruction congressman, and collector of customs for Charleston. His journey from bondage to political prominence embodied the radical democratization of the postwar South and the era's fragile promise of Black citizenship.

Smalls was born enslaved in Charleston. During the Civil War, he commandeered the Confederate steamship Planter and sailed it to Union lines, becoming a symbol of enslaved heroism. After the war, he was elected to the South Carolina House of Representatives in 1868 and then to Congress from 1875 to 1879, serving during the height of Reconstruction.

Smalls purchased his former master's plantation and served as mayor and port collector of Charleston, accumulating wealth and influence in the postwar South. His legislative work focused on securing Black land ownership and suffrage, advocating for voting rights, education, and economic opportunity for freedmen. He witnessed the Democratic restoration, known as Redemption, which ended Reconstruction and disenfranchised Black voters. In 1895, he authored My Life on the Water, a memoir recounting his escape and rise, establishing himself as a living bridge between enslavement and freedom.
